title: Inside the Hidden Consumer Crisis with Lakshmi Ganapathi
summary: Lakshmi Ganapathi argues that inflation, BNPL dependence and opaque credit structures reveal strain hidden by benign bank statistics. She connects these concerns to shorts in FICO, Wingstop, AutoZone, Group 1 and DoorDash. Eisman challenges the missing bank-loss evidence, adopts selected Wingstop and refinancing explanations, and distinguishes near-term noise from future software-loan maturities. Inflation and several BNPL figures are supported, while claims about universal borrower distress, payment-network invisibility and automatic private-company markdowns overreach. Most company-specific causal claims remain unverified, and 2027 refinancing outcomes are genuinely unfinished.
assessment: Useful tension between household surveys and reported bank outcomes, with several independently verified premises. Neither survey dependence nor public-equity drawdowns alone establishes hidden bank losses or a universal private valuation decline. Guest positions, Eisman's probing questions and his explicit recap endorsements are kept separate.
speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_01 is Steve Eisman and SPEAKER_00 is Lakshmi Ganapathi, inferred with high confidence from the introduction, questions, replies and final recap. Dialogue determines brief interjections.
framework_points: Separate household hardship from bank loan performance.
Distinguish payment status, expected-loss provisions and realized charge-offs.
Use consistent survey denominators and distinguish any use from dependence.
Trace private-credit funding, guarantees and retained exposure.
Compare private companies with public peers without assuming identical equity and enterprise-value changes.
Make maturities and sponsor incentives explicit.
Demand cohort evidence for immigration and affordability explanations.
tools_and_charts: Bank earnings calls and nonaccrual balances
CPI, PPI, energy inflation and real wages
Warehouse lines and synthetic risk transfers
Software equity drawdowns and loan maturity ladders
Receivables, invoice factoring and used-car auction observations
transcript_cautions: The episode was published May 27, 2026; references to released April inflation data imply recording after May 13, without establishing an exact day.
The speaker immediately corrects HSBC billions to millions; the corrected amount is used.
The Wingstop demographic denominator changes from customers to store locations and is not silently reconciled.
Technology and food-delivery survey percentages differ from the inspected originating survey; delivery is not exclusively DoorDash.
Public software equity losses are not identical to enterprise-value losses.
Statements about corporate fraud remain allegations unless adjudicated.
The opening promotional summary is not used in place of the complete discussion.

claims.claim: The First Brands collapse involved fraud through duplicated collateral or invoices and diversion of money by its leadership.

evidence.title: First Brands executives charged

evidence.title: Quarterly Banking Profile Q1 2026
evidence.finding: Asset quality remained generally favorable. Noncurrent balances rose 3.3% quarterly to $134.3 billion while the past-due and nonaccrual rate fell three basis points to 1.53%; provisions were $21.4 billion.

evidence.title: 2026 BNPL survey and tracker
evidence.finding: Core survey: 47% paid late within a year; groceries 29% versus 14% in 2024; rent 13%; technology 34%; clothing 39%; delivery/takeout 20%. Convenience and credit access also motivate use.

claims.next_check: Track matched bank and household indicators rather than treating survey distress as realized bank loss.
